blocks.text:
Design a Concert Ticketing System where fans buy general-admission tickets for a specific section of a venue. Unlike assigned seating, a section simply has a fixed capacity, once it fills up, new requests join a first-come-first-served waitlist, and a cancellation automatically promotes the next waiting fan.

  • Actors: fans purchasing tickets, and fans on a waitlist for a sold-out section.
  • Scope: one concert with multiple capacity-based sections (no individual seat numbers).
  • Goal: guarantee a section is never oversold, and that a cancelled ticket is always offered to the longest-waiting fan first.

The one rule this entire system exists to enforce: a section can never sell more tickets than its capacity, and any freed-up spot always goes to whoever has been waiting the longest. Everything else builds on top of that.

items: The system shall let a fan purchase a ticket for a named section, if capacity remains.
The system shall automatically add a fan to a waitlist if the requested section is already full.
The system shall support cancelling a ticket, freeing up one spot in that section.
A cancellation shall automatically promote the longest-waiting fan on that section’s waitlist, if anyone is waiting.
The system shall notify listeners of every purchase, waitlist join, and promotion.

metadata.alt: Four non-functional priorities: no overbooking, fairness, extensibility and observability

items: No overbooking: a section’s tickets sold must never exceed its capacity, under any circumstance.
Fairness: the waitlist must be honored in strict first-come-first-served order, never out of turn.
Extensibility: new pricing tiers and new sections must be addable without rewriting the purchase flow.
Observability: every purchase, waitlisting, and promotion must be visible to anything watching the system.
Thread Safety: two fans requesting the last spot in a section at nearly the same moment must never both succeed.
Should the waitlist have a maximum size, or can it grow without bound?
When a fan is promoted from the waitlist, do they need to confirm within a time window, or is the ticket immediately theirs?
Should different sections support different pricing, and should pricing be able to change as a section fills up?
Do we need to support a fan being on multiple sections’ waitlists simultaneously?
Is a single concert enough, or does the design need to support many concurrent concerts?
A promoted fan’s ticket is immediately confirmed, no separate confirmation window is modeled in this core design.
This design implements a fixed TieredPricingStrategy, the pricing mechanism itself is pluggable for future strategies like surge pricing.
The waitlist has no maximum size in this design, real systems would likely cap it and discussed separately.
A fan can only be on one waitlist entry per section in this simplified model, duplicate joins are not explicitly prevented here and are called out in Common Mistakes.
This design covers a single concert, a real system would layer a Concert/Venue hierarchy above it, discussed in Improvements.

metadata.alt: TicketingService composing Sections (each owning its own waitlist), a PricingStrategy, and notifying TicketingObservers

items: Section: a named area with a fixed capacity, a sold count, and its own FIFO waitlist.
PricingStrategy: however a section’s ticket price gets decided.
TicketingObserver: anything that wants to react to a purchase, waitlisting, or promotion.
TicketingService: the orchestrator running the purchase and cancellation-promotion flow.

metadata.alt: TicketingService managing multiple Sections, each owning its own waitlist queue

items: Composition: TicketingService composes its Section objects, they have no purpose outside the specific concert being managed.
Composition: each Section composes its own waitlist queue, the queue’s entire lifecycle is tied to that one section.
Association: TicketingService is associated with a PricingStrategy and zero or more TicketingObservers, both swappable independently.
Realization: TieredPricingStrategy realizes PricingStrategy; ConsoleTicketingObserver realizes TicketingObserver.

metadata.alt: TicketingService tying together Section, PricingStrategy and TicketingObserver

blocks.text: Notice that the waitlist queue lives entirely inside Section, not inside TicketingService. This keeps each section’s fairness guarantee self-contained and independently correct.
Two patterns, plus one structural mechanic, keep this design correct and extensible.

metadata.alt: PricingStrategy as the shared contract behind a fixed-tier strategy and a future surge-pricing strategy

blocks.text: Why needed: different concerts and different sections need different pricing rules, and pricing may eventually need to respond to demand. Why best: TicketingService only ever calls pricingStrategy.getPrice(section), never hardcoding a price itself. What it solves: lets pricing evolve independently of the purchase and waitlist logic.

metadata.alt: TicketingService notifying every registered TicketingObserver of purchases, waitlisting, and promotions

blocks.text: Why needed: a real system needs to send confirmation texts, update a live sold-out indicator, and notify promoted fans, all reacting to the same events. Why best: new observer types can be added freely with zero changes to the core purchase flow. What it solves: keeps every notification concern fully decoupled from the actual ticketing rules.
9.3 The Waitlist as a FIFO Queue
blocks.content: 9.3 The Waitlist as a FIFO Queue

metadata.alt: A full section routing new requests to a FIFO waitlist, with cancellations promoting from the front of that same queue

blocks.text: Using a genuine first-in-first-out queue (not a list requiring manual sorting) is what makes the fairness guarantee trivial to implement correctly: the fan who has been waiting longest is always exactly the one at the front, promoted with a single O(1) operation.

items: Section: responsibility is tracking capacity, sold count, and its own waitlist. Attributes: name, capacity, ticketsSold, waitlist. Methods: hasSpace(), sellOneTicket(), releaseOneTicket(), addToWaitlist(), pollWaitlist(), hasWaitlist().

TicketingService: responsibility is running the purchase and cancellation-promotion workflow. Attributes: sections, pricingStrategy, observers. Methods: purchaseTicket(), cancelTicket(), addObserver().

metadata.alt: PricingStrategy and TicketingObserver as the two extension points, each with one concrete implementation shown

blocks.text: PricingStrategy isolates how a price is calculated. TicketingObserver isolates reactions to the three events fans and operators actually care about: a sale, a waitlisting, and a promotion.
Three workflows matter most: a normal purchase, joining a waitlist, and a cancellation triggering a promotion.

metadata.alt: A fan purchasing a ticket while the section still has capacity remaining

blocks.text: The capacity check and the actual sale happen as one uninterrupted step, this is exactly what section 16 discusses protecting under concurrent access.

metadata.alt: A fan being added to the waitlist because the requested section is already completely full

blocks.text: Joining the waitlist is treated as a legitimate, successful outcome, not an error, the fan is given a clear place in line rather than simply being turned away.

metadata.alt: A cancelled ticket immediately freeing a spot that is then automatically given to the longest-waiting fan

blocks.text: The promotion happens as part of the exact same cancellation operation, there is no separate background process required for a fan to move from waitlisted to confirmed.

metadata.alt: The purchase decision: sell immediately if there is room, otherwise join the waitlist

items: Happy path, direct purchase: the section has room, the ticket sells immediately and the fan is notified of a confirmed purchase.
Happy path, waitlisted: the section is full, the fan joins the waitlist and is notified they are waiting, not rejected outright.
Happy path, promotion: a cancellation occurs while fans are waiting, the longest-waiting fan is automatically promoted to a confirmed ticket.
No-op case: a cancellation occurs with an empty waitlist, the spot simply stays open for the next new purchase request.
TicketingService.purchaseTicket(userId, sectionName): the single entry point for buying a ticket, returns whether a ticket was actually sold immediately.
TicketingService.cancelTicket(sectionName): releases one sold ticket and triggers waitlist promotion if applicable.
TicketingService.addObserver(TicketingObserver): registers a new observer for ticketing events.
Section.hasSpace(): the core capacity check every purchase decision is built on.

metadata.alt: A purchase request for an unknown section name being rejected before any state changes

items: Invalid input: a purchase or cancellation request for a section name that does not exist is rejected immediately, with no state changes anywhere.
Resource unavailable: not directly applicable to the in-memory version, a persisted variant would need to handle a failed save gracefully.
Business-rule violation: a section can never be sold beyond its capacity, hasSpace() is checked before every single sale, with no code path that bypasses it.
System failure: a broken ticketing observer throwing an exception should be caught per-listener, never allowed to prevent a valid purchase or promotion from completing.

metadata.alt: Two fans requesting the last remaining spot in a section, guarded by a lock around the entire capacity-check-and-sell sequence

blocks.text: purchaseTicket() reads section.hasSpace() and then calls sellOneTicket() as two separate steps, if two requests for the last spot run concurrently, both could see hasSpace() return true before either actually sells. The entire check-and-sell sequence must be synchronized per section (a lock scoped to that Section instance, not the whole service, for better throughput across different sections).

items: Adding surge pricing (price rising as a section approaches capacity) requires only a new PricingStrategy implementation, zero changes to TicketingService.
Adding an SmsNotificationObserver that texts a promoted fan is a pure TicketingObserver implementation.
Supporting a confirmation window for promoted fans (must confirm within 10 minutes or lose the spot) would add a timestamp and a background sweep, without changing the core promotion logic.
Future work: layering a Venue and multiple simultaneous Concert entities on top would let one system manage many events, reusing this exact per-section flow unchanged.
Single Responsibility: Section only tracks capacity and its own waitlist, TicketingService only orchestrates the purchase and promotion workflow.
Open/Closed: new pricing strategies and observer types can be added without modifying TicketingService’s existing, already-correct logic.
Liskov Substitution: any PricingStrategy or TicketingObserver implementation can be substituted freely without TicketingService needing to know which one it has.
Interface Segregation: PricingStrategy exposes exactly one method, TicketingObserver exposes exactly the three events it genuinely needs.
Dependency Inversion: TicketingService depends on the PricingStrategy and TicketingObserver abstractions, never on a specific concrete implementation.
A section with capacity zero: every purchase request immediately goes straight to the waitlist, never sells even one ticket.
A cancellation on a section that never sold any tickets: ticketsSold would go negative, a real implementation should guard against cancelling more tickets than were ever sold.
The exact same fan requesting a section twice while already waitlisted: without extra tracking, they could end up with two waitlist entries, called out explicitly in Common Mistakes.
A promotion happening when the waitlist has exactly one fan: after promotion, hasWaitlist() correctly returns false, and the next cancellation simply leaves the spot open.
Section.hasSpace() / sellOneTicket() / releaseOneTicket(): O(1), simple field checks and updates.
Section.addToWaitlist() / pollWaitlist(): O(1), a queue’s enqueue and dequeue are both constant time.
TicketingService.purchaseTicket() / cancelTicket(): O(1) overall, dominated by a single hash map lookup plus the section’s own O(1) operations.
Space: O(number of sections) plus O(current waitlist size) per section.

metadata.alt: CONCERT containing SECTION rows, each with sold TICKET records and queued WAITLIST_ENTRY rows

blocks.text: CONCERT stores the event itself, SECTION tracks capacity and current sold count per named area, TICKET records each confirmed sale, and WAITLIST_ENTRY preserves queue order explicitly via queue_position, so the fairness guarantee survives even across a server restart.

items: How would you add a confirmation window for promoted fans, automatically moving to the next waitlisted fan if they do not confirm in time?
How would you prevent the same fan from joining one section’s waitlist multiple times?
How would you extend this design to support a Venue managing many concurrent Concerts, each with its own sections?
How would you scale the per-section lock across multiple servers without it becoming a bottleneck during a high-demand on-sale moment?

items: Why does the waitlist live on Section rather than as one global waitlist on TicketingService? Because fairness is a per-section guarantee, a fan waiting for GA should never be affected by demand for VIP, keeping the queue scoped to its own section makes that isolation automatic.

Why use a queue instead of a list you sort by timestamp? Because a queue gives O(1) enqueue and dequeue by construction, sorting a list by timestamp on every promotion would be needlessly slower and more error-prone.

Why is joining the waitlist treated as a legitimate outcome rather than a failure? Because from the fan’s perspective, being placed in a fair queue for a sold-out section is meaningfully different from being rejected outright, the design’s observer events reflect that distinction explicitly.

An alternative could sell tickets on a strict lottery basis instead of first-come-first-served, fairer in spirit for extremely high-demand events, but a materially different (and more complex) allocation mechanism than what this design implements.

A simpler design could reject purchases outright once a section is full, with no waitlist at all, much simpler, but loses the ability to automatically fill cancellations with genuinely interested fans.
Using a shared, cross-section waitlist would let a fan wait for "any available section," a reasonable variant, but complicates fairness since sections likely have very different demand levels.
Persist every section, ticket and waitlist entry (already modeled in the ER diagram) so an on-sale event survives a server restart without losing queue order.
Add a confirmation window with automatic re-promotion for fans who do not respond in time, to avoid a promoted spot sitting unclaimed indefinitely.
Rate-limit purchase attempts per user during high-demand on-sale moments to keep the system responsive under load.
Expose a read-only "spots remaining" API separately from purchaseTicket(), so a UI can show live availability without risking accidental mutation.
